statement: Kokopelli is best documented in current scholarship as a modern composite/commercial image rather than a straightforward transmission of a single traditional figure. A peer-reviewed source, "Deciphering Kokopelli: Masculinity in Commodified Appropriations of Native American Imagery," Communication and Critical/Cultural Studies 4(3) (2007), analyzes contemporary Kokopelli imagery as a projection of "Euro-American masculinist fantasy" built on "the trope of the primitive," stating the modern figure "tells us more about tourism, marketing, and Euro-American culture than the indigenous cultures of the Southwest." The popular commercial Kokopelli prototype appears to derive from a Hohokam pottery design (a different, related but distinct Southwestern archaeological culture), not a Hopi-specific origin, despite marketing association with Puebloan cultures broadly — a documented case of pan-Southwest flattening across genuinely distinct cultural traditions, exactly the "Hopi vs. Pueblo generally" conflation this batch is built to avoid.

sources.citation: "Deciphering Kokopelli: Masculinity in Commodified Appropriations of Native American Imagery." Communication and Critical/Cultural Studies 4(3), 2007.

does_not_demonstrate: That the popular commercial Kokopelli figure is a reliable, uncommercialized representative example of specifically Hopi religious iconography
